headline: The Dow passes 2,000 as shares soar 13 percent in January
text: The Dow Jones average closed above 2,000 for the first time on 8 January, and shares kept climbing all month to new highs. The S&P 500 rose 13% in January to 274.08, its biggest monthly gain since at least 1975.
imageCaption: President Reagan works on his State of the Union address in the Oval Office, 23 January 1987

headline: Computer shares lead a January surge
text: The Nasdaq index rose 12% in January to 392, and computer companies rose far more: Microsoft about 52%, Intel 49% and Apple 37%. Personal computers built on Intel's new 386 chip, the first from Compaq since September, are on sale, and investors are betting on a recovery after the chip slump of 1985 and 1986.

headline: Tokyo passes 20,000; IBJ soars
text: Japan's Nikkei 225 index closed above 20,000 for the first time on 30 January, up from about 13,000 a year earlier. The Bank of Japan has cut its discount rate four times since January 1986, to 3%, and cheap money is pushing up shares and land prices. The cuts are meant to cushion exporters from the soaring yen: the dollar, which bought about 240 yen just before the Plaza agreement of September 1985, now buys about 153. IBJ shares rose 69% in January.

headline: Schlumberger loses 2 billion dollars, its first loss ever
text: Schlumberger's accounts for 1986 show a loss of 2.02 billion dollars, the first loss since it listed in 1962, after fourth-quarter charges of 1.74 billion, mainly writing off goodwill at Sedco Forex and Dowell Schlumberger and writing down drilling rigs. Excluding the charges and Fairchild, it earned 84 million. Oil fell from 24 dollars in January 1986 to as low as 7 in July; the number of active North American drilling rigs halved, and North Sea rig rates fell from 90,000 dollars a day in 1981 to 12,000.
source: Schlumberger 1986 annual report, chairman's letter and financial highlights (auditors' report dated 12 February 1987), https://investorcenter.slb.com/static-files/e7c50ea0-e56c-47f8-8877-7b7e04938ad9 (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Offshore drilling platforms under construction in a shipyard

headline: America imposes trade sanctions on Japan over chips
text: On 17 April President Reagan raised tariffs on $300 million of Japanese exports to the US, saying Japan had broken the semiconductor agreement of September 1986 by dumping chips in other countries and keeping its own market closed. It is the first US trade retaliation against Japan since the war. The dollar fell below 140 yen this month, although six countries agreed at the Louvre in Paris in February to stop its fall and the Bank of Japan then cut its rate to 2.5%, the lowest in its history.

headline: A German teenager lands a small plane next to Red Square
text: On 28 May Mathias Rust, an 18-year-old amateur pilot from West Germany with about 50 hours of flying experience, landed a rented Cessna on a bridge next to Red Square in Moscow. He had flown from Helsinki through Soviet air defences without being stopped. He was arrested two hours later.
imageCaption: Mathias Rust, in a red flying suit, beside his Cessna next to St Basil's Cathedral in Moscow, 28 May 1987
imageCredit: press photograph of 1987 (agency not named by the page)

headline: Apple pays its first dividend
text: On 11 May Apple declared its first dividend. The Macintosh Plus and the new Macintosh II with colour are selling well to businesses, designers and schools, and the Mac with Apple's LaserWriter printer has become the tool for desktop publishing.
imageCaption: The Macintosh II, introduced in March 1987

headline: US warships escort Kuwaiti tankers; the UN demands a ceasefire
text: The US Navy began escorting Kuwaiti tankers re-registered under the American flag through the Gulf, and on 24 July the first convoy's tanker Bridgeton struck a mine. On 20 July the UN Security Council unanimously passed Resolution 598 demanding an immediate ceasefire between Iran and Iraq; Iraq accepted, Iran has not. On 31 July a clash between Iranian pilgrims and Saudi police in Mecca left 402 dead, 275 of them Iranians, by Saudi count; Iran says the police opened fire.

headline: Edzard Reuter to lead Daimler-Benz
text: Werner Breitschwerdt is stepping down as chairman of Daimler-Benz; Edzard Reuter, the board member for planning who arranged the purchases of MTU, Dornier and AEG, will succeed him on 1 September. Deutsche Bank's chief Alfred Herrhausen backed the choice. Reuter wants to forge the car maker and its new subsidiaries into an integrated technology group. The company is worth about 47.6 billion marks on the stock market.
source: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edzard_Reuter (read 2026-10-03); Mercedes-Benz Classic, Illustrated Chronicle 1987 ('Edzard Reuter becomes Chairman of the Board of Management', 1 September 1987), https://mercedes-benz-publicarchive.com/marsClassic/en/instance/ko/1987.xhtml?oid=4911147 (read 2026-10-03); Der Spiegel 31/1995, https://www.spiegel.de/spiegel/print/d-9205712.html (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Edzard Reuter, who became chairman of Daimler-Benz in 1987, speaking in St. Gallen in 1988

headline: Shares hit a record as Greenspan takes over the Fed
text: The S&P 500 closed at a record 336.77 on 25 August and the Dow at 2,722.42, both up more than a third since New Year. Alan Greenspan was sworn in on 11 August as chairman of the Federal Reserve, taking over from Paul Volcker with the dollar weak and interest rates rising. Volcker leaves after eight years in which inflation fell from a peak of 14.8 percent in March 1980 to 3.9 percent (July), and the 10-year Treasury yield from 15.3 percent in September 1981 to 8.8 percent in August.
imageCredit: While provided by the Bureau of Engraving and Printing, it is a Federal Reserve image.

headline: Dirty Dancing opens
text: The dance film Dirty Dancing, with Patrick Swayze and Jennifer Grey, opened in American cinemas on 21 August. The small studio Vestron made it on a low budget.

headline: Black Monday hits the high-flyers hardest
text: On Monday 19 October the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 508 points, or 22.6%, its worst day ever. Wal-Mart shares had already dropped 11.7% on Friday 16 October. Stocks that had risen most, such as Wal-Mart, were among the hardest hit; on 20 October the Federal Reserve promised to supply cash to the banking system.
imageCaption: A trader holds his head on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange as panic selling sweeps Wall Street, 19 October 1987
imageCredit: Maria Bastone / AFP - Getty Images file

headline: Black Monday: the S&P 500 falls 20 percent in a day
text: After a bad trade deficit report on 14 October pushed interest rates up, shares fell 9% in a week; then on Monday 19 October the Dow plunged 508 points or 22.6% and the S&P 500 20.5%, the largest one-day falls in their history. Blamed are the dollar and the trade deficit, rising interest rates, a public row between Treasury Secretary Baker and Germany over the dollar, a bill to curb tax breaks for takeovers, and 'portfolio insurance' programs that sold automatically as prices fell. On 20 October the Fed said it stood ready to supply cash to the financial system; markets around the world crashed too, and the S&P 500 ended October down 22% at 251.79.
imageCredit: Mark Carlson, US Federal Reserve Board of Governors

headline: No relief after the crash: the dollar slides and shares fall another 9 percent
text: Markets stayed unsettled after the October crash, with wide price swings and flights to safety. The dollar fell about 5% against the other big currencies, and the S&P 500 lost another 9% in November to 230.30, about 32% below its August record.
imageCaption: Brokers on Wall Street in the weeks of the crash, New York, autumn 1987

headline: 1987 in review: up 2 percent, after the wildest year in memory
text: The S&P 500 ended 1987 at 247.08, up 2% on the year, after rising 39% to its August record and then losing a third of its value in two months. The Dow closed at 1,938.83, up 2.3%. So far the crash has had little visible effect on business activity, and interest rates are lower than before it.
imageCaption: Traders on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange watch the monitors on Black Monday, 19 October 1987
imageCredit: AP / Corbis / Getty Images / The Canadian Press (collective credit printed for the page's photographs)

headline: Reagan and Gorbachev sign the INF treaty
text: President Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev signed the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty in Washington on 8 December. It removes all American and Soviet land-based missiles with ranges of 500 to 5,500 kilometres, including the Pershing II and cruise missiles in western Europe and the Soviet SS-20s, with inspections on both sides. At Reykjavik in October 1986 the two leaders had come close to far deeper cuts but parted over Reagan's missile shield.
